solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Embracing sum rounded to significant figures in physics?

indicators.note: rounded suggests the letters are turned about and reshaped into something new

explanation.surface: A maths lesson about rounding a total to the right number of significant figures for a physics answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rounded' looks like the arithmetic of rounding off, but it signals that the letters of EMBRACING SUM are rearranged. In nuclear physics these are nucleon counts (2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) that make nuclei unusually stable.
explanation.definitionFit: Physicists give that name to the nucleon totals that complete a nuclear shell, figures of special significance.

clue.text: Lunch box, no ham? Do get upset!

indicators.note: to upset something is to knock it over, so these letters are tipped into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone opens a lunch box, finds no ham, and is told to go ahead and be cross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lunch box' is British slang for a man's genitals, so it is not about food at all. The letters of NO, HAM and DO are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunch box is cheeky British slang for the male genitals, which is also a euphemistic sense of the answer.

clue.text: Great header, City's goal in first- half — winning start for City

indicators.note: header says this abbreviation leads, standing at the head of the answer

parts.note: G is a standard abbreviation for great, as in GB for Great Britain
LA is the usual abbreviation for the city of Los Angeles, and the possessive adds the S

indicators.note: the first half of the word goal is its opening two letters
only the start of the word winning is kept, so the rest after its opening letter goes

parts.note: the word winning as written

explanation.surface: A football report: a great header gives the City side a first-half goal and a winning start.
explanation.walkthrough: The football words are all mechanism: 'header' puts G at the head, 'first- half' keeps half of goal, and 'start' keeps the front letter of winning. Glasgow is Scotland's largest city.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasgow is a large city in western Scotland, so the bare word city defines it as an example.

clue.text: Types of jumper in which man drinks

parts.note: to man a ship is to crew it
to neck a drink is British slang for gulping it down

explanation.surface: A question about which kinds of sweater a man wears while drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man' is a verb here, as in manning a boat. A jumper is the British word for a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweater with a round, close-fitting collar is named for its neckline, one style among many jumpers.

clue.text: Cavalryman in National Hunt set-up

indicators.note: set-up says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters sit inside the words National Hunt

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A horseman riding in National Hunt racing, Britain's jump-racing season.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft had no indicator for the hidden letters; 'in' is that indicator. In a down clue 'set-up' means read upwards. National Hunt is British steeplechase and hurdle racing.
explanation.definitionFit: An uhlan was a lancer in the Polish, Prussian or Austrian cavalry, so a mounted soldier.

clue.text: Sailing ship docked before many turned up in port

indicators.note: to dock is to cut short, as with a tail, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a brig is a two-masted sailing ship

indicators.note: in a down clue turned up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: lots means many

explanation.surface: A sailing ship ties up before crowds turn out at the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'docked' looks nautical but means cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Bristol is a historic seaport city in south-west England on the Avon, so a port.

clue.text: About to let loose

parts.note: re means about or concerning
to let property is to lease it out

explanation.surface: Something is on the point of being set free.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'about to' as 'on the verge of', but 'about' and 'to let' are separate pieces and 'loose' alone is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to loose something is to set it free, as when an archer frees an arrow.

clue.text: Seat in city area

parts.note: Chester is a cathedral city in Cheshire, England
a field is an area, as in a field of study or open ground

explanation.surface: A place to sit somewhere in an urban district.
explanation.walkthrough: Chesterfield is also an English town, which adds to the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep-buttoned leather sofa with arms level with its back is a classic piece of furniture to sit on.

clue.text: Toxic growth of gas in French bean stews

parts.note: H is the chemical symbol for hydrogen, a gas
en is the French for in

indicators.note: stewing mixes things up, so the letters of bean are jumbled

explanation.surface: A poisonous plant turns up amid French bean stews.
explanation.definitionFit: Henbane is a poisonous plant of the nightshade family, so a toxic growth.

clue.text: Reduced to inactivity, face the other way and look west

indicators.note: facing the other way means the word is turned round back to front

parts.note: a dial is the face of a clock or watch
lo is an old word meaning look

explanation.surface: Someone, flattened by events, turns away and gazes westward.
explanation.definitionFit: Being laid up by illness or misfortune leaves a person incapacitated and out of action.

clue.text: Spring tide journalist experienced

parts.note: a spring is a well, a source of water
tide is an old word for season, as in Yuletide
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A journalist with long experience reporting on spring tides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring tide' looks like one phrase about high tides, but the words split: a spring is a WELL and 'tide' means a season, as in Eastertide.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone thoroughly seasoned has long practice and know-how, like timber dried over time.

clue.text: Drink makes lines go fuzzy

indicators.note: fuzzy means blurred and out of shape, so these letters lose their order

explanation.surface: Alcohol makes the lines you read go blurry.
explanation.definitionFit: A liqueur made by steeping blackthorn fruit in gin is a British alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Girl holds bat, playing game

indicators.note: holds means the girl's name wraps around the other piece

parts.note: Nell is a girl's name

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters of bat are moved about

explanation.surface: A girl grips a bat while playing a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bat' looks like the sports equipment the girl is holding, but it is just letters to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Netball is a team sport played with a ball and a high ring, popular in British schools.

clue.text: Fund that's in 19 down!

indicators.note: that's in tells us the answer sits inside the cross-reference once it is spelt out, so the letters around it are dropped

parts.note: the cross-reference written out in words is nineteen down

explanation.surface: A fund that is in fashion, since 19 down refers to another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The reference seems to send you to 19 down (FASHION), but the answer lies within the words 'nineteen down' spelt out: nineteEN DOWn. Written as digits the letters are not on the page, so the parse trims NINETE and the final N.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a college or charity a permanent income is to provide it with money, to finance it.

clue.text: People who sing about posh cars

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means about
Rollers is slang for Rolls-Royces, the luxury cars

explanation.surface: Singers whose songs are about expensive cars.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas singers who go door to door with seasonal songs are a kind of singer.

clue.text: Tie Stranraer lost, the Gunners having gone for it

indicators.note: lost in the sense of confused and astray, so the letters are rearranged
one thing going for another means a swap: the gunners leave and the other word takes their place

parts.note: Stranraer is a Scottish port town with a football club
RA, the Royal Artillery, are the gunners

explanation.surface: A football report: Stranraer lost a cup tie, the Arsenal side going for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Gunners' looks like Arsenal football club, but means RA. Swapping RA for IT in STRANRAER leaves STRANERIT, which is then rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie is a restriction or constraint, something that holds a person back.

clue.text: Those supporting legend after split

parts.note: split legend into leg end, and the end of a leg is a foot
rests are things that support, as a rest for a cue

explanation.surface: Followers who back a famous figure after a break-up.
explanation.walkthrough: Divide 'legend' into 'leg end': the end of the leg is the FOOT. The whole clue then also describes the answer, things that hold up the end of the leg.
explanation.definitionFit: Stools or bars on which a seated person props their feet support the lowest part of the leg.

clue.text: Working daily, in theory

parts.note: on means working, as a machine that is switched on
a daily is a newspaper published every day

explanation.surface: Someone works on a daily newspaper, at least in principle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something true only as written down, not in practice, holds in principle rather than reality.

clue.text: Rovers' football team

definitions.meaning: rovers are wanderers, people who roam the countryside
Glasgow's ... are a famous Scottish football club

explanation.surface: Naming the football team of a club called Rovers.
explanation.walkthrough: Many British clubs are called Rovers, which steers you towards a club name, but 'Rovers' is a plain definition here.
explanation.definitionFit: Rangers roam an area, so they are wanderers, and the Glasgow club is a well-known side.

clue.text: Content of gut showing one of the early signs of flatulence?

definitions.text: Content of gut showing one of the early signs of flatulence?

parts.words: Content of gut showing one of the early signs of flatulence?
parts.note: the microbes living in the intestine are named with the word for plant life, and they also make up the first letters of the word flatulence

explanation.surface: A medical note about gut contents and the onset of wind.
explanation.walkthrough: The gut's bacteria go by this name, and the opening letters of 'flatulence' are F, L, A, which with O and R make it look like an early part of that word.
explanation.definitionFit: Gut flora is the standard term for the community of microbes living in the digestive tract.

clue.text: Make way

definitions.meaning: to make something, to shape or form it
a way or manner of doing something

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to step aside, but the two words are separate definitions, a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To fashion is to shape or create, and a fashion is also a manner or mode of doing something.

clue.text: Not in 19 down? Shock, horror!

parts.note: out means not in, as away from home
19 down is fashion, and a rage is a craze or fashion

explanation.surface: Indignation at being out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 down is FASHION; 'all the rage' means fashionable, so RAGE is a fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: Outrage is shocked indignation, the reaction mocked by the tabloid cry of shock, horror.

clue.text: Lays out dead writer (died Saturday or Sunday)

parts.note: ex means former, no longer living, so dead
a pen is something that writes
D is the abbreviation for died in records
S abbreviates either weekend day

explanation.surface: An undertaker lays out a dead author who died at the weekend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lays out' looks like preparing a body, but means spends.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay out money is to spend or use it up.

clue.text: Geese flying east in film

indicators.note: in means the compass letter goes inside the word for a thin layer

parts.note: a film is a thin skin or layer on a surface

explanation.surface: Geese flying east appear in a nature film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'film' is not a movie but a thin layer.
explanation.definitionFit: A V-shaped formation of wild geese in flight is called a skein, a collective noun.

clue.text: When cooked, it's perhaps given stir too

definitions.text: When cooked, it's perhaps given stir too

indicators.note: cooking turns raw ingredients into something new, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A kitchen note: this dish, while cooking, may get a stir as well.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of STIR and TOO, cooked up, give the dish, which is indeed stirred constantly as it cooks.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian rice dish cooked slowly in stock needs frequent stirring, which is the whole clue's picture.

clue.text: Pail expert emptied in river or drain

indicators.note: in says those outer letters go inside the river's name

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and another in Wales and England

indicators.note: emptied means the insides of both words are taken out, leaving their outer letters

explanation.surface: Emptying a bucket expertly into the river or down the drain.
explanation.definitionFit: To drain something is to use it up or exhaust its supply.

clue.text: Follow as a model has topless stint at tea dances

indicators.note: topless means the first letter is taken off

parts.note: to stint is to restrict or limit

indicators.note: dances suggests the letters of tea move around

parts.note: the word tea as written

explanation.surface: A model works a topless shift at a tea dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stint' is a synonym, LIMIT, before its top comes off; 'at' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To copy someone, treating them as an example to be followed, is to mimic them.

clue.text: Bit of grammar now taught on the radio?

parts.note: present means now, the current moment

indicators.note: on the radio means the word is heard rather than read, so its sound counts

parts.note: the word taught said aloud is taut, which means tense or stretched tight

explanation.surface: Grammar now being taught on a radio programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taught' when spoken sounds like 'taut', meaning stretched tight.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb form for current actions is one of the basic parts of grammar.
